Spearheaded by principal investigator Frank Keutsch and his team, including David Keith, the experiment sought to refine computer models that assess the risks and benefits of solar geoengineering, specifically solar radiation management. It was crucial to note that SCoPEx was not designed to deploy geoengineering techniques or cool the planet.

The experiment involved a scientific balloon gondola operating at an altitude of around 20 kilometers, releasing a minuscule amount of calcium carbonate—between 100 grams and 2 kilograms—into a one-kilometer-long, 100-meter-diameter plume. A test flight planned for 2021 in Sweden, intended to assess the hardware, was postponed by the SCoPEx Advisory Committee for societal engagement, with no particles released. In March 2024, Harvard announced that Keutsch would no longer pursue SCoPEx, with the platform likely to be repurposed for unrelated stratospheric research. This project remains separate from conspiracy theories surrounding "chemtrails," which are not supported by scientific evidence.
